transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/time: 2026-12-22 15:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Sørensen (CTO, Fjord), Marco Ruiz (ML Eng, Fjord), Priya Iyer (Head of DevOps, Fjord)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be fuzzy):
Fjord is evaluating Redwood for a mix of hosted and private deployments. Primary concerns are context length (8k vs 16k vs 32k), multilingual inference (Nordic + Spanish), and tool-calling for structured lab data access. They asked about dedicated pools for steady throughput, V P C/private control plane options, and encryption/K M S integrations. Next steps include pricing, latency estimates, and security docs.

Topics: model selection, context length, multilingual support, tool-calling (APIs to their ELN), VPC/private deployment, SOC2/KMS, pricing and pilot scope

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, this is Maya from Redwood. Ravi's here with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Lena: Hi Maya, doing well. Thanks. We, uh, have been looking forward to this — lots on the plate before Q1.
[00:10] Ravi: Great. Quick agenda. We'll do a short discovery on your workloads, then walk model choices for hosted vs dedicated vs private, then talk about tool-calling and security. Sound good?
[00:18] Marco: Yep. That works. We'll mostly be answering questions and then figuring out a pilot scope.
[00:22] Maya: Perfect. To get started, can you give a quick overview of the primary product flows you want to power? The parts that need long context, and any latency targets?
[00:30] Lena: Sure. Two main things: one is an R&D assistant for scientists — they paste long lab notes, sometimes whole experimental histories — so we need a lot of context. We think 16k might be minimum, some runs might need 32k. Second is a customer-facing summarization for support where it's usually short, like a few hundred tokens, but strict p95 latency requirement around 400 to 700 ms.
[00:48] Priya: Right, and from infra side we care about data residency — some datasets must remain in our EU V P C, and we need audit logs for all requests. We also use an internal ELN and want the model to call a tool that retrieves structured entries and returns citations.
[00:59] Ravi: Great, that helps. A couple clarifying q's: what's your typical qps for the R&D assistant during work hours? And are you expecting heavy concurrency or mostly single-user interactive sessions?
[01:10] Marco: It's mostly interactive. Think 30–50 concurrent users at peak, each doing a handful of requests per minute. For the R&D assistant, the sequence length distribution is very skewed — 80% under 8k, 15% between 8k and 16k, and about 5% hit 32k. But those 32k ones are important.
[01:29] Maya: That's useful. For the 32k tail, we typically recommend a hybrid approach: either run a longer-context model in Dedicated or Private where you can reserve capacity and avoid cold start plus KV caching, or chunk/recall older parts of the context using prefix caching.
[01:41] Marco: Can you explain prefix caching in plain terms?
[01:44] Ravi: Yeah — so we keep the KV cache for the active window and store older context in a compacted summary. When the model needs older tokens, we can rehydrate from the summary or retrieve the original chunk — it's a tradeoff between latency and accuracy. The runtime supports automatic prefix/K V caching so you don't have to manage individual caches.
[02:00] Lena: And for the clinical notes, accuracy's important; summaries might lose subtle experimental detail. So we don't want aggressive summarization.
[02:08] Maya: Understood. For accuracy-sensitive R&D workflows, many teams go with Dedicated or Private so they can pin to a model variant and control quantization profiles. Hosted is great for quick start and lower overhead, but Dedicated gives predictable throughput and Private gives VPC controls.
[02:23] Priya: On Private — can you run the control plane in our V P C? We have air-gapped environments for some projects.
[02:29] Ravi: Yes, we offer a Private deployment with a customer-managed control plane — option for on-prem package for air-gapped needs. That includes K M S/H S M integrations and full audit log export. There are some onboarding steps for network setup and we usually coordinate with your infra team.
[02:41] Priya: Good. For K M S — do you support AWS K M S, Azure Key Vault and HSM?
[02:46] Maya: We integrate with AWS K M S, Azure K V, and we have HSM partner integrations for enterprise customers. We'll share the security pack.
[02:54] Marco: Ok about models — we were comparing several open models. For Nordic languages we saw good perf in Mistral clones and some Llama 3 variants. What does Redwood recommend for multilingual with strong few-shot and tool-calling reliability?
[03:09] Ravi: For multilingual and tool-calling, we look for models with robust instruction-following and tokenizer coverage. A common path: start with a 16k-capable open model (quantized variant) for dev and evaluation — run evaluations on your prompt set. If tool-calling with strict citation is required, we often recommend the model be run with a dedicated runtime config that preserves provenance tokens and structured outputs. Redwood's model catalog can suggest verified variants and quantization profiles.
[03:33] Lena: Do you have examples of models in the catalog for Nordic+Spanish?
[03:37] Maya: Yes, we have curated variants flagged for multilingual coverage — I'll share the model catalog link. Off the cuff, Mistral-based 16k variants and some Llama 3 16k variants have good coverage, but for lab jargon you might need fine-tuning or a retrieval-augmented approach.
[03:52] Marco: About tool-calling — we'd like the model to call a 'get_experiment' tool that returns structured JSON with timestamps and measurements. How is structured output handled?
[04:01] Ravi: Two parts: function/tool calling at the runtime level — the model emits a call intent, and Redwood provides deterministic post-processing to ensure outputs are JSON schema-compliant. Second, we can store call logs and attach citations so each generated statement can be traced back to source entries. There can be occasional mis-attribution in noisy inputs but we provide audit trails.
[04:18] Lena: That audit trail is critical. Can you keep that in our V P C and integrate with our SIEM?
[04:23] Maya: Yes. For Private deployments audit logs can be exported directly to your SIEM endpoints. For Hosted we provide secure log export options but with different retention SLAs.
[04:31] Priya: Networking: we have NATed egress and strict outbound policy. Will Redwood's Private still need inbound ports?
[04:37] Ravi: For the customer-managed control plane we typically require outbound authenticated tunnels to a management endpoint; we avoid inbound holes where possible. We'll surface the exact port recommendations in the network onboarding doc.
[04:48] Marco: Pricing — curious tradeoffs. If we go Dedicated with reserved capacity for steady workload vs Hosted pay-as-you-go, what are the typical delta in $/token?
[04:58] Maya: Ballpark: Dedicated reserved gives a meaningful reduction on steady-state per-token and per-inference cost, maybe 25–45% cheaper depending on commit and model family. Hosted is higher per-token but lower upfront and easier for spikes. We'll send an apples-to-apples sheet.
[05:12] Marco: For the R&D assistant, latency matters — our p95 target 700 ms for short queries. Do you have p95 numbers for 16k models on Hosted?
[05:20] Ravi: It depends on model size and hardware. For a quantized 16k-capable model on our hosted instance, p50 might be ~180–300 ms for short prompts, p95 could be ~500–900 ms depending on concurrency. On Dedicated with reserved GPU pools and optimized batching you can tighten p95. We'll run a quick estimate for your concurrency profile.
[05:41] Lena: Would you also recommend a hybrid: Hosted for support summaries and Dedicated for R&D?
[05:46] Maya: That's a common pattern — use Hosted for customer-facing lower-context flows to reduce ops, and Dedicated/Private for sensitive high-context workflows. Redwood supports routing policies so you can route by route or by model tag.
[05:57] Priya: Any compliance certifications we should know about out of the box? SOC 2 Type II was mentioned earlier?
[06:02] Maya: Yes, we maintain SOC 2 Type II and have ISO alignment. For Private deployments we can support additional controls and attestations. We'll include the SOC2 report in the security pack.
[06:11] Marco: On evaluation — we'll share a small prompt set with typical long-form docs and some lab queries. What's needed to run a pilot?
[06:19] Ravi: For a pilot we usually need: 1) sample prompts + expected outputs, 2) a small dataset for retrieval/ELN integration, 3) an infra contact for network setup if Private or Dedicated, and 4) target SLOs and success metrics. Then we can spin up a short-term Dedicated pool or use Hosted with pinned model variants.
[06:34] Lena: Timeline: we'd like a pilot by mid-January. Is that realistic?
[06:38] Maya: Yes. If we get your prompts and the infra info this week, Ravi and I can scope a pilot and share a statement of work.
[06:45] Marco: We have one more technical nit: tokenization differences across models cause subtle content shifts. For the lab tables with units, integer rounding matters. Any guidance?
[06:54] Ravi: Good point. Tokenization and numeric stability can vary. For determinism we recommend fine-tuning or calibration sets and use the same model variant in the pilot as in prod. Also, structured output enforcement via tool-calling can reduce ambiguity — e g, force numeric fields to be typed as numbers.
[07:09] Priya: Are there any known limitations with tool-calling under high concurrency with Dedicated pools?
[07:15] Ravi: No fundamental limitations; it's mostly about throughput engineering. Tool-calling does add a bit of orchestration overhead — function calls are serialized in the request flow — but with dedicated capacity and batching we can keep latency SLOs. We'll propose config settings.
[07:27] Maya: Quick recap before we close: we heard — primary need long context (16k/32k tail), multilingual Nordic+Spanish, tool-calling to ELN with structured JSON and citations, data residency in EU VPC, SOC2/KMS and audit export, pilot by mid-Jan. Is that accurate?
[07:44] Lena: Yes that's right.
[07:45] Marco: Yep.
[07:46] Priya: Correct.
[07:47] Maya: Next steps again: I'll send pricing + model catalog + security pack by 12/24. Ravi will run latency/cost estimates for 16k/32k tails and propose either Dedicated sizing or Hosted tuning by 1/4. Priya will share V P C diagram and egress patterns by 1/5.
[07:59] Priya: We'll do that.
[08:01] Lena: Also we'll attach sample prompts to the CRM record.
[08:04] Maya: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with a short SOW and scheduling for a technical deep-dive if needed.
[08:12] Marco: Thanks, bye.
[08:13] Maya: Bye.
